title: Baby Christening Shawl in Openwork Lace
subtitle: Lace weight dc mesh with shell border, 100cm square, adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet
excerpt: A 100cm square christening shawl worked in fine lace weight yarn on a 2.5mm hook. The body is an open dc mesh worked in rows; the border is a deep shell lace edging. Construction follows a traditional pattern from Weldon's Practical Crochet, now in the public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A regular open grid formed by alternating double crochets with chain-1 spaces. The next row's dc sits above the chain space of the previous row, creating a net-like fabric.

A decorative edging worked by placing multiple treble crochets into a single chain space to form fan shapes. In this pattern the border is worked in rounds around all four sides of the finished mesh square.
A small decorative loop formed by chaining 3 or 4 stitches and slip stitching back into the base stitch. Used at the tips of shells in the border for a scalloped finish.

content.text: This shawl is a 100cm square worked in lace weight yarn on a 2.5mm hook. The body is a flat dc mesh: alternating double crochets and chain-1 spaces worked in rows, producing a fine open net. A four-round shell lace border is then worked around all four sides in joined rounds. The pattern is adapted from a christening shawl construction documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet, a late nineteenth-century needlework series now in the public domain. The project is rated advanced because of the fine gauge, the long row count, and the precision needed during blocking to achieve a square finish. The stitches themselves are all foundational: if you are confident with dc and treble in DK weight, the techniques are the same here but with a much finer yarn.

A word on blocking: lace weight crochet changes dramatically when blocked. The mesh opens up, the border shells spread into fans, and the square settles flat. Budget time for a proper wet-block before assessing the finished size. Rust-proof pins and a foam mat are essential, not optional, for this pattern.

Yarn: approximately 400g of lace weight yarn (a 2-ply cotton or wool-silk blend is traditional for christening shawls; cotton holds its shape well after blocking). Hook: 2.5mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, tape measure, a foam blocking mat, and rust-proof pins. At least 50 pins are recommended for blocking the full border.
Gauge

One dc mesh repeat (1 dc, ch 1) measures approximately 0.6cm wide and 0.6cm tall on a 2.5mm hook. The body mesh square is approximately 85cm x 85cm before the border, which adds approximately 7.5cm on each side. Work a swatch of at least 30 mesh repeats and measure carefully: a difference of even 0.1cm per repeat becomes 16cm over a full 167-repeat row.
Stitches used
ch: chain
sl st: slip stitch
dc mesh: dc, ch 1, skip 1, repeat
tr: treble crochet (UK)
dtr: double treble crochet (UK)
Shell border: 5 tr in ch sp for the body of each fan
Picot: ch 3, sl st in base st
Pattern
Body mesh: foundation chain
Ch 337. This gives 168 mesh repeats (ch 2 per repeat = 336 chs, plus 1 turning ch). The foundation chain should measure approximately 85cm laid flat.
Body mesh Row 1
Ch 4 (counts as dc + ch 1), skip 1 ch, dc in next ch, [ch 1, skip 1 ch, dc in next ch] to end, turn. (168 dc, 168 ch-1 sps)
Body mesh Rows 2 onward
Ch 4 (counts as dc + ch 1), skip first ch-1 sp, dc in next dc, [ch 1, skip ch-1 sp, dc in next dc] to end, working final dc into 3rd ch of turning ch, turn. (168 dc, 168 ch-1 sps)
Repeat this row until the mesh square measures approximately 85cm x 85cm, approximately 142 rows at stated gauge. Fasten off.
Border round 1: base round

Join yarn in any corner ch-1 sp. Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc evenly along each side: 1 dc per ch-1 sp along row ends, 1 dc per ch-1 sp along foundation and final row. Work 3 dc into each corner. Sl st to join. (approximately 680 dc total: 168 per side plus 4 corner groups of 3)
Border round 2: shell placement

Ch 3 (counts as first tr), skip next dc, [5 tr in next dc, skip 2 dc, dc in next dc, skip 2 dc] across each side, placing a 7-tr corner shell into each corner centre dc. Sl st to join. (approximately 45 shells per side plus 4 corner shells)
Border round 3: picot tips
Sl st to centre tr of first shell, ch 1, dc in same tr, picot (ch 3, sl st in base dc), [dc in centre tr of next shell, picot] across each side and at each corner. Sl st to join. (1 picot per shell)
Border round 4: final picot row
Work a final round of dc between each picot with a further picot at each dc. This gives a double-picot border edge. Fasten off.
Finishing

Weave in all ends on the wrong side. Wet-block the shawl by soaking in cool water for 20 minutes, removing excess moisture in a towel, and laying flat on a foam mat. Pin the four corners to 100cm square, then pin along each side edge at approximately 5cm intervals. Pin each border shell open so it fans fully. Leave to dry completely, which may take 24 hours or more depending on the fibre. Do not remove pins until the fabric is entirely dry.
Care
Hand wash in cool water with a gentle detergent suitable for the fibre. Rinse well. Dry flat, reshaping as needed. Re-block if the square loses its shape after washing. Do not tumble dry.
What to try next

The dc mesh technique in this pattern is the foundation for all filet crochet: a dc-and-chain grid where filled squares form images and open squares form the background. For a simpler lace shawl using the same yarn weight but a larger hook for a more open mesh, see the mohair lace shawl. The shell border worked in rounds here is the same technique used in the baby shell stitch shawl, but at a much finer scale.
